title: Suffixes on verbs

objectives.can: Identify a pronominal object suffix on a verb.

explanation.summary: A verb can carry a pronoun on its end: 'he made me know', 'he set it up', 'he will deliver you'. In the Aramaic of the Bible this happens in about sixty-four verb forms, mostly in the causative stems and in the imperfect. The suffix is the object of the verb, and the imperfect puts a connecting נ before it.

sections.heading: What a suffix on a verb is
body: You met the pronominal suffixes on nouns and prepositions in A1.2.3: they mean 'my', 'your', 'his' on a noun, and 'me', 'you', 'him' on a preposition. On a verb the same set of endings is the object: 'me', 'us', 'you', 'him', 'it', 'her'. The corpus marks it with the feature Suffix, whose value says which person the suffix stands for: 1cs (me), 1cp (us), 2ms (you, singular), 2mp (you, plural), 3ms (him, it) and 3fs (her, it).

The suffix tells you who or what receives the action. In הוֹדַעְתַּנִי the verb is 'you made known' and the suffix is 'me': 'you have made me know'. The verb carries two kinds of person: the doer (marked by the Person, Gender and Number of the verb itself) and the object (marked by the Suffix).

Only six suffixes occur on verbs in the texts. There is no suffix for 'them' on any verb, and none for 'you' (feminine). When the object is 'them', Aramaic uses a separate pronoun, as in Daniel 2:35: the wind carried them away, וּנְשָׂא הִמּוֹן.

Meaning on a verb
Added to a perfect or imperative

sections.heading: Suffixes on the perfect, the imperative and the infinitive
body: On the perfect and the imperative the suffix is added straight onto the verb, and the vowels before it shift. A perfect third masculine singular with a suffix often ends in -ֵהּ or -ַהּ: אֲקִימֵהּ 'he set it up' (Daniel 3:1, an Aphel), הֲקִימֵהּ 'he set him up' (Haphel, Daniel 5:11), שָׂמֵהּ 'he placed it' (Peal), וְחַתְמַהּ 'and he sealed it' (the king sealed the stone, which is a feminine noun). The third masculine plural with -הִי: הַקְרְבוּהִי 'they brought him near'.

A second person perfect keeps its personal ending before the suffix: הוֹדַעְתַּנִי 'you made me know' and הוֹדַעְתֶּנָא 'you made us know' are both Haphel perfects, second masculine singular. The 1cs suffix is -נִי, the 1cp is -נָא. An imperative takes the same: הַחֲוֺנִי 'declare to me!' (plural) and הַעֵלְנִי 'bring me in!' (singular).

An infinitive can also carry a suffix. A Haphel infinitive with its object: לְהוֹדָעֻתַנִי 'to make me know', לְהוֹדָעוּתָךְ 'to make you know', or the Shaphel לְשֵׁיזָבוּתֵהּ 'to deliver him', לְשֵׁיזָבוּתַנָא 'to deliver us'. With a Peal infinitive the suffix may be the doer rather than the object: וּכְמִקְרְבֵהּ in Daniel 6:21 means 'and when he drew near'. Context decides which.

sections.heading: Suffixes on the imperfect: the connecting נ
body: The imperfect, with its person letters, does not take a suffix directly. Between the verb and the suffix Aramaic puts a נ, which is doubled when it stands between two vowels. That gives the endings you see on most suffixed imperfects: -ִנַּנִי, -ֻנַּנִי (1cs), -ִנֵּהּ, -וּנֵּהּ (3ms), -ִנַּהּ (3fs), -ִנָּךְ (2ms), -ְכוֹן with a נ before it (2mp).

So יְהוֹדְעִנַּנִי is the Haphel imperfect third masculine singular, 'he will make me know' (Daniel 7:16): the stem, then the connecting נּ, then the suffix -נִי. אֲהוֹדְעִנֵּהּ is the Haphel imperfect first singular, 'I shall make him know' (Daniel 5:17). יִתְּנִנַּהּ is the Peal imperfect of נְתַן, 'he gives it' (Daniel 4:22). The doubled נ does not belong to the root or to the suffix: it is the join.

The imperfect stem is also changed by its ending. In a plural, the nun of the ending -וּן drops and the connecting נ takes its place: יְבַהֲלוּנֵּהּ 'they will alarm him' (Daniel 5:6). A few imperfects take a suffix with no connecting נ at all: יְבַהֲלָךְ 'he will alarm you' (Daniel 4:16) and יְבַהֲלוּךְ 'they will alarm you' (Daniel 5:10).

sections.heading: 'To him' is not 'him'
body: Aramaic often does not put the pronoun on the verb at all. The person who is addressed or who benefits is usually given by לְ with a suffix, as a separate word: אֲמַר לֵהּ 'he said to him' (Daniel 2:25), יְהַב לֵהּ 'he gave to him'. In Daniel 2:48 both patterns stand side by side: the king gave him gifts (יְהַב לֵהּ, with לֵהּ 'to him'), and made him ruler (וְהַשְׁלְטֵהּ, with a suffix 'him' on the verb). A suffix on the verb is a direct object; לְ plus a suffix is an indirect object or a 'for' phrase.

The same endings also appear on participles used as nouns: יָעֲטֹהִי 'his counsellors' and לְשָׂנְאָךְ 'to those who hate you'. Here the suffix is possessive, as on a noun. The corpus tags them with the same Suffix feature as it does an object suffix, so read the sense.

misunderstandings: The suffix is not the subject. הוֹדַעְתַּנִי means 'you made me know', not 'I made you know'. The person of the verb itself says who acts; the suffix says who is acted on.
A doubled נ in the middle of an imperfect is not part of the root. It is the connecting נ between the stem and the suffix, as in יְהוֹדְעִנַּנִי.
-ֵהּ on a verb means 'him' or 'it'. Do not read it as the possessive 'his' that it is on a noun. Look at the part of speech before you decide.
A suffix like -ַהּ may mean 'it' with a feminine noun: וְחַתְמַהּ is 'sealed it' where 'it' is the stone.

deeper.heading: The connecting נ
body: Grammarians call this נ the 'energic' or 'connecting' nun, and some compare it with a similar nun in other Semitic languages. Whether it once added emphasis is a matter of debate. In the Aramaic of the Bible it is simply the usual way to join an imperfect to a suffix.

examples.analysis: Two Haphel perfects of יְדַע, both second masculine singular, with an object suffix. הֽוֹדַעְתַּנִי (12) has the suffix -נִי, 'me': 'you have made me know'. הוֹדַעְתֶּנָא (19) has the suffix -נָא, 'us': 'you have made us know'. The personal ending -תְּ belongs to the verb, and the suffix is added after it.

quoted.english: Then Daniel answered and said before the king: 'Let thy gifts be to thyself, and give thy rewards to another; nevertheless I will read the writing unto the king, and make known to him the interpretation.

examples.analysis: אֲהוֹדְעִנֵּהּ is a Haphel imperfect, first person singular, of יְדַע, with the suffix -הּ, 'him' or 'it': 'I shall make it known' to the king. The נּ between the stem and the suffix is the connecting נ. The prefix אֲ- is the first person of the Haphel imperfect.

examples.analysis: Two Pael imperfects with the suffix of the first person singular. וִידַחֲלִנַּנִי (2) is the Pael imperfect, third masculine singular, 'and it made me afraid'. יְבַהֲלֻנַּנִי (8) is the Pael imperfect, third masculine plural, 'they alarm me'. Both have the connecting נּ followed by -נִי, and the second also keeps the ending -וּ of the plural (written ֻ).

examples.analysis: יְהַב (7) is the Peal perfect of 'give'. לֵהּ (8) is a separate word: לְ with the suffix of the third masculine singular, 'to him'. וְהַשְׁלְטֵהּ (9) is a Haphel perfect of the verb 'rule', third masculine singular, with the suffix -ֵהּ as its object: 'and he made him ruler'. The first pronoun is attached to a preposition, the second to the verb.

examples.analysis: Two infinitives with an object suffix, both meaning 'to deliver him'. לְשֵׁיזָבוּתֵהּ (12) is a Shaphel infinitive with the suffix of the third masculine singular. לְהַצָּלוּתֵהּ (18) is a Haphel infinitive with the same suffix, from another verb with a similar sense. The infinitive has the lengthened ending -וּת before the suffix.

quoted.english: And a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'it', the stone, as a feminine singular object
check.explain: The suffix is the third feminine singular and refers to the stone, a feminine noun. A noun that is a thing may be 'it' in English.

reading.why: Daniel's thanks and his entry before the king: 'you have made me know', 'you have made us know', 'bring me in', and the king's question about 'making me know' (לְהוֹדָעֻתַנִי), so four suffixed verbs of the first person fall within four verses.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: I thank Thee, and praise Thee, O Thou God of my fathers, who hath given me wisdom and might, and hast now made known unto me what we desired of Thee; for Thou hast made known unto us the king's matter.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Therefore Daniel went in unto Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon; he went and said thus unto him: 'Destroy not the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will declare unto the king the interpretation.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said thus unto him: 'I have found a man of the children of the captivity of Judah, that will make known unto the king the interpretation.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: The king spoke and said to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar: 'Art thou able to make known unto me the dream which I have seen, and the interpretation thereof?'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)
